rejected.title: Collecting data
card: Survey
asking people questions, such as how they travel to school. It collects what people say or choose.
Measurement
using a tool to find a number, such as a height in cm or a time in seconds.
Observation
watching and recording what happens, such as counting cars that pass a school gate in one hour.
Biased sample

a sample is the group you collect data from. If it leaves out some people or favours one type, it is biased and can give a wrong picture. Example: asking only the school netball team about favourite sports.
rejected.remember: Choose the method to suit the data. A sample should fairly match the whole group.

a.q: A student wants to know how many cars pass the school gate between 8 am and 9 am. Which method fits best?
opts: Observation, counting the cars as they pass
Survey, asking students what cars they own
Measurement, finding the length of each car
Biased sample, asking only the teachers
a.why: Counting cars as they pass is watching and recording what happens, so it is observation. A survey would record what students say, not what actually passes the gate.
a.clue: The student watches and records what happens.

b.q: Jo wants to know the favourite lunch of all students at her school. She asks only the students in the canteen queue. Why might the results be wrong?
opts: The sample leaves out students who do not use the canteen
A survey cannot collect data about what people choose
The answers were found with a tool instead of by asking
The sample includes every student in the whole school
b.why: Students who bring lunch from home are left out, so the sample may not match the whole school. That makes it biased. A survey suits this question, since it collects what people choose, so the method is not the problem.
b.clue: Who is missing from the group Jo asked?

a.q: A council worker wants to know how many people walk through a park between 12 pm and 1 pm. Which method fits best?
opts: Observation, counting the people as they walk past
Survey, asking people how often they visit parks
Measurement, finding the width of the park path
Biased sample, asking only people who own dogs
a.why: Counting people as they walk past is watching and recording what happens, so it is observation. A survey would record what people say about visits, not who actually walks through in that hour.
a.clue: Think about whether the worker needs answers, a tool reading, or a count of real events.
